strengths: The paper identifies a real and useful problem: group-wise attribution for diffusion model outputs, where instance-level attribution is often the wrong granularity for styles/classes and LOGO retraining is too expensive.

The LOGO-based estimand is clearly stated, and using ELBO differences as a practical likelihood surrogate gives the method a coherent scoring rule. The distinction between the counterfactual target and semantic similarity baselines is well motivated.

The empirical setup includes both a controlled CIFAR-10 proof of concept and a more realistic Stable Diffusion/UnlearnCanvas style-attribution setting. The paper also compares against multiple relevant baselines, including CLIP similarity, gradient-based attribution, and an unlearning-based instance attribution method.

The appendices provide many implementation details, hyperparameters, timing breakdowns, metric definitions, and ablations for the CIFAR ReTrack configuration, which helps reproducibility more than is typical for this topic.

The computational results are practically meaningful: on CIFAR-10 the method is much faster than LOGO and substantially faster than gradient-based methods, while on UnlearnCanvas it is faster than LOGO and far faster than per-query instance unlearning.
weaknesses: The central causal-attribution claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The gold standard is LOGOA, but in the Stable Diffusion experiment LOGOA is itself only a fine-tuning proxy from SD 1.5, not a true model trained without the style from pretraining. Since SD 1.5 likely already contains many artistic styles, the claimed counterfactual “style absent from training” is not actually realized.

The empirical gains are modest in important places. On CIFAR-10, GUDA top-1 is 0.727 versus DAS at 0.716 and NDCG@3 is 0.677 versus 0.675, so the accuracy advantage over a strong attribution baseline is negligible; the main benefit there is speed. On UnlearnCanvas, GUDA improves top-1 over CLIPA, but CLIPA is essentially free and remains fairly close on NDCG@3, making the practical tradeoff less decisive than the narrative suggests.

There is no uncertainty quantification across seeds, model initializations, query sets, or LOGO/unlearning runs. Given the small UnlearnCanvas evaluation size (320 generated images over only 16 alphabetically selected styles) and close CIFAR margins, confidence intervals or repeated runs are needed to judge whether the reported differences are reliable.

The conditional GUDA-C method is much less theoretically supported than GUDA-U. The anchor-style redirection objective is intuitive, but the paper does not establish that it approximates the conditional LOGO optimum; it is validated only empirically against a limited LOGO proxy.

The CIFAR full-model training protocol is unusual: the all-group model excludes one random class per epoch to exposure-match LOGO models. This changes the meaning of the “full” model and may confound the intended comparison to a model trained on all groups.

The evaluation is primarily fidelity to LOGOA rankings, not validation against independent ground truth of actual data contribution or downstream usefulness in copyright/fair compensation/debugging scenarios. Thus the work demonstrates approximation of a chosen proxy more than reliable real-world attribution.

The UnlearnCanvas selection of 16 styles alphabetically from 60 is not well justified, and metrics are computed only over this subset even though models are trained in a 60-style world. This may make the ranking task easier or at least different from the stated large-group attribution setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite strong hyperparameter detail: the manuscript does not clearly state code/model release availability, and the experiments require substantial GPU resources and many trained diffusion checkpoints. Baseline reimplementations also leave room for implementation-dependent conclusions.

The impact/ethics discussion is brief relative to the application domain. The paper acknowledges privacy/legal risks, but does not give concrete guidance on misuse, uncertainty communication, or the risk of over-interpreting group attributions as legally meaningful evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: group-level attribution for diffusion outputs, which is relevant to copyright, compensation, dataset debugging, and model transparency.
The LOGO framing is conceptually useful: defining group attribution through a leave-one-group-out counterfactual makes the desired estimand clearer than many similarity-based attribution proxies.

The manuscript includes nontrivial engineering effort, including CIFAR-10 LOGO models, Stable Diffusion/UnlearnCanvas experiments, timing breakdowns, several ranking metrics, and implementation details in the appendix.
The method is computationally attractive relative to full LOGO retraining, and the reported wall-clock reductions are potentially useful if the approximation is valid.
weaknesses: The main theoretical justification appears unsound. Appendix A claims that one can sample noisy points from the forget distribution while preserving an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only LOGO objective, but changing the sampling distribution from p_ret to p_for without an appropriate density-ratio correction does not in general yield the same objective. This directly undermines the claimed alignment between GUDA-U/ReTrack redirection and LOGO retraining.

The empirical gains are overstated. On CIFAR-10, GUDA is only marginally better than DAS on Top-1, MRR, NDCG@3, and Top-3, and is worse on Spearman; the claimed substantial improvement is not supported by the numbers. CLIPA is also much cheaper and surprisingly competitive, so the practical advantage is narrower than presented.

The evaluation uses LOGOA, an ELBO-difference surrogate, as the gold standard, but the paper does not validate that LOGOA corresponds to meaningful causal attribution for generated samples. Since both the target and GUDA score are based on related ELBO computations, the evaluation may partly measure agreement with a constructed surrogate rather than externally validated attribution quality.

The CIFAR-10 setup compromises the stated estimand: the so-called all-group model excludes one random class per epoch to exposure-match LOGO models, so it is not a straightforward model trained on all groups. This makes the counterfactual interpretation less clean and could affect attribution rankings.

The UnlearnCanvas result is weak in absolute terms: 45.6% Top-1 agreement over only 16 evaluated styles, with Spearman 0.239. The paper presents this as strong evidence, but it still misses the LOGOA top style more often than not, and evaluation is restricted to an alphabetically selected subset rather than the full 60-style setting.

There is no statistical uncertainty analysis. The paper reports single numbers without confidence intervals, standard deviations, significance tests, or multiple seeds, despite small margins on CIFAR-10 and stochastic training/unlearning procedures.

The conditional GUDA-C method is largely heuristic. The CLIP-weighted anchor construction, descriptor extraction via Qwen2.5-VL, prompt synthesis, and style swapping are plausible engineering choices, but they lack a convincing derivation showing that they approximate the conditional LOGO counterfactual.

Baseline comparisons are not fully persuasive. Instance-level attribution methods are adapted to group-level ranking in ways that may not be optimal, while CLIPA is intentionally simple. The paper needs stronger baselines, fuller hyperparameter parity, and analysis showing that baseline failures are not due to implementation or aggregation choices.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many appendix details. The descriptor extraction pipeline, exact prompts to the VLM, selected style subset rationale, random seeds for training/unlearning, code, checkpoints, and complete hyperparameter search protocol are not sufficiently specified for independent reproduction.

The limitations and impact discussion are too brief. The paper does not adequately discuss reward/score hacking analogues, failures when groups overlap, benchmark contamination, false attribution in legal settings, or privacy risks from extending group attribution toward instance attribution.

Originality is moderate at best. The paper mostly combines LOGO-style counterfactual attribution with existing diffusion unlearning ideas and ELBO scoring. Given the limited novelty, acceptance would require much stronger theoretical and empirical support than the manuscript currently provides.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and practically important problem: group-wise training-data attribution for diffusion models, where users often care about styles, classes, or data-provider groups rather than individual examples. The LOGO-style counterfactual framing is clear and well motivated.

The core idea of using unlearning to approximate leave-one-group-out counterfactual models is natural and useful. The paper is careful to define GUDA as an approximation to a counterfactual estimand rather than claiming certified deletion, which improves the soundness of the framing.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for this problem: CIFAR-10 provides a controlled unconditional setting with 10 class groups, while UnlearnCanvas with Stable Diffusion 1.5 tests a more realistic conditional text-to-image style-attribution setting.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial and practically meaningful. On CIFAR-10, GUDA reduces total wall-clock time from 207:47 for LOGOA to 2:02, and on UnlearnCanvas from 46:08 to 8:54, while preserving much of the LOGOA ranking signal.

The presentation is generally strong. The paper distinguishes the estimand, the oracle approximation, and the practical unlearning approximation; it also provides detailed appendices on training settings, ELBO estimation, metrics, and ablations.
The impact discussion is appropriate and acknowledges both positive uses for transparency/fair compensation and potential privacy or legal misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central evaluation depends on LOGOA as a gold standard, but the oracle itself is only a practical proxy in the large-scale setting: UnlearnCanvas LOGO models are fine-tuned from Stable Diffusion rather than trained from scratch. This is reasonable computationally, but it weakens claims that GUDA approximates the true group-removal counterfactual.

The advantage over strong baselines is mixed. On CIFAR-10, DAS is very close to GUDA in accuracy (Top-1 0.716 vs. 0.727; NDCG@3 0.675 vs. 0.677), so the main benefit there is efficiency rather than substantially better attribution quality. On UnlearnCanvas, GUDA improves over CLIPA, but absolute Top-1 agreement remains modest at 0.456.

The conditional GUDA-C method is more heuristic than the unconditional ReTrack-based version. The style-anchor redirection is plausible, but its relationship to the LOGO counterfactual is not as theoretically grounded, and the paper would benefit from stronger ablations of anchor selection, prompt construction, and descriptor extraction.

The evaluation scope is still limited to object classes and artistic styles with disjoint group definitions. The paper explicitly leaves overlapping groups and other group notions to future work, which limits the generality of the contribution for real data provenance settings.

The paper uses ELBO differences as the attribution score, but the manuscript acknowledges that ELBO does not necessarily preserve likelihood ordering. More analysis of score stability, variance across timestep/noise samples, and sensitivity to the ELBO approximation would strengthen soundness.

Reproducibility is good in terms of hyperparameter reporting, but not complete from the manuscript alone. It is unclear whether code, generated prompts/descriptors, trained checkpoints, and all LOGO/unlearned models will be released, which matters because the experiments are expensive to reproduce.

Originality is solid but not exceptional. The work combines known components: LOGO attribution, unlearning, ELBO scoring, and CLIP/style anchors. The contribution is useful as a framework and empirical study, but the methodological novelty is incremental rather than transformative.

strengths: The paper formulates a clear group-wise attribution target for diffusion models via LOGO-style counterfactual removal and distinguishes this from instance-level attribution and semantic similarity. This is a useful problem framing for settings such as class/style attribution where practitioners care about groups rather than single examples.

The proposed GUDA framework is conceptually simple and well motivated: approximate each group-removed counterfactual model by unlearning from the full model, then score influence by an ELBO difference. The connection to ReTrack in the unconditional case gives the method a plausible link to the retain-only objective.

The evaluation includes an explicit LOGO oracle on CIFAR-10 and a practical LOGO fine-tuning proxy for Stable Diffusion/UnlearnCanvas, plus comparisons to CLIP similarity, DAS, D-TRAK/TRAK, ESD-style unlearning, and Wang et al. (2024). The paper reports both attribution quality and wall-clock cost, which is important for the claimed computational advantage.

The appendix is unusually detailed: it gives model/training hyperparameters, ELBO estimation protocols, baseline implementation details, metric definitions, ablations over unlearning and anchor choices, timing breakdowns, a PF-ODE likelihood check for the ELBO proxy, and a noisy-partition robustness study.

The limitations section is honest and identifies real issues, including the non-guaranteed ordering induced by ELBO differences, dependence on unlearning approximation quality, disjoint group assumptions, non-additivity, and limited experimental scope.
weaknesses: The central empirical target is fidelity to LOGOA, which is itself a constructed oracle based on ELBO differences rather than an externally validated notion of causal contribution. The paper partly addresses this with PF-ODE likelihood checks, but the main conclusions still depend strongly on accepting this estimand as the right attribution target.

The empirical gains are meaningful but not decisive. On CIFAR-10, GUDA only slightly improves over DAS on Top-1 and NDCG@3, while DAS is comparable on several metrics and Spearman is slightly higher. On UnlearnCanvas, GUDA improves over CLIPA, but Top-1 remains only 45.6%, indicating substantial mismatch to the oracle even in the controlled 16-style setting.

The Stable Diffusion LOGO oracle is a fine-tuning-from-pretrained proxy rather than true training without the group from scratch. This is pragmatic, but it weakens the counterfactual interpretation, especially because pretrained SD may already contain the target styles and because removing one UnlearnCanvas style during fine-tuning may not remove that style knowledge from the base model.

Scalability is only partially demonstrated. GUDA reduces cost relative to LOGO, but still requires one unlearned model per group and ELBO evaluation under each group model. This may become expensive for hundreds or thousands of groups, and the paper does not explore compression, caching, or approximate search over groups.

The conditional text-to-image unlearning component is more heuristic than the unconditional ReTrack-based case. The weighted style-selection anchor is plausible and ablated, but there is no strong theoretical argument that it approximates the conditional LOGO objective, and its dependence on CLIP/Qwen-derived descriptors may introduce hidden biases or dataset-specific tuning.

The UnlearnCanvas evaluation is limited to the first 16 alphabetically selected styles and 320 generated queries, while models are trained over 60 styles. This makes the large-model experiment useful but still narrow; it is unclear whether results hold for harder, more overlapping, or non-style group definitions.

Reproducibility is mostly strong in terms of details, but the abstract says “code is available at” without an actual link in the extracted manuscript. If code/checkpoints are not released, reproducing the many trained, LOGO, unlearned, and baseline models would be costly.

The ethics discussion is minimal beyond a conflict-of-interest statement and motivating use cases such as copyright/fair compensation. Since attribution outputs could affect legal or compensation decisions, the paper should more explicitly discuss uncertainty calibration, failure modes, and risks of over-interpreting noisy group attribution scores.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and underexplored problem: group-level attribution for diffusion-generated outputs, which is more practically aligned with styles/classes than instance-level attribution alone.
The LOGO-style counterfactual estimand is clearly motivated, and the distinction between the desired oracle target and the unlearning approximation is mostly explicit.

The manuscript includes useful implementation detail, timing breakdowns, ablations for unlearning hyperparameters/anchor choices, and an honest limitations section noting ELBO proxy issues, unlearning approximation bias, disjoint-group assumptions, and non-additivity.
The computational motivation is real: replacing per-group retraining with unlearning gives substantial speedups in the reported CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas settings.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the central claims. Most evaluation measures agreement with the paper’s own LOGO/ELBO oracle, rather than validating attribution against an independent notion of true data influence. This makes the evaluation partly self-referential: the method is designed to approximate LOGO, then judged mainly by similarity to LOGO.

The gains are often modest. On CIFAR-10, GUDA’s Top-1 is 0.727 versus 0.716 for DAS, and NDCG@3 is 0.677 versus 0.675. Under the PF-ODE likelihood oracle in Appendix D.5, DAS/D-TRAK are competitive or better on broader ranking metrics, weakening the claim that GUDA is clearly superior beyond head identification.

The main realistic experiment is limited. UnlearnCanvas evaluates only 16 alphabetically selected styles out of 60, only 320 queries, and uses a practical fine-tuning LOGO proxy rather than true retraining. GUDA’s Top-1 agreement is only 0.456, which is better than baselines but still quite low for a method presented as reliable group attribution.

The conditional text-to-image method is heuristic. The anchor construction relies on CLIP-weighted style substitutions and descriptor extraction, but there is no theoretical connection comparable to the unconditional ReTrack derivation, and no likelihood-oracle validation analogous to CIFAR-10.

Reproducibility is concerning: the abstract says “The code is available at” but no URL is provided. The experiments also require many trained/unlearned diffusion models and generated descriptors, so missing code/checkpoints materially affects reproducibility.

The comparison set is incomplete in the strongest setting. On UnlearnCanvas, the paper compares against CLIPA and Wang et al. but not the stronger gradient-based baselines used on CIFAR-10, making it hard to know whether GUDA’s advantage persists in the text-to-image regime.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper suggests GUDA identifies primary contributing groups “more reliably,” but the reported alignment with LOGO is imperfect, dataset scope is narrow, and the approach depends heavily on the quality of the unlearning operator.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: group-wise, counterfactual training-data attribution for diffusion models, where instance-level attribution or semantic similarity is often the wrong abstraction for questions about styles, classes, or contributors.

The LOGOA estimand is clearly motivated as a leave-one-group-out counterfactual, and the paper is careful to distinguish the oracle target from GUDA’s unlearning-based approximation. This improves conceptual clarity relative to attribution methods that conflate similarity, influence, and deletion effects.

The empirical design is stronger than many attribution papers: GUDA is evaluated against explicit LOGO oracles on both CIFAR-10 and a Stable Diffusion/UnlearnCanvas style-attribution setting, with multiple baselines, head-focused ranking metrics, timing analysis, ablations, and an ELBO-vs-PF-ODE likelihood sanity check.

The results support the main practical claim that unlearning can approximate LOGO attribution much more efficiently: about 100x speedup over LOGOA on CIFAR-10 and about 5.2x on UnlearnCanvas, while improving Top-1/head metrics over CLIPA and instance-level unlearning baselines.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The paper explains the difference between unconditional ReTrack-style redirection and conditional anchor-based redirection, and the appendices provide useful implementation details, hyperparameters, ablations, and limitations.

The limitations section is unusually honest and appropriate: it acknowledges ELBO ordering issues, lack of approximation-error bounds, disjoint group assumptions, non-additivity, and limited experimental scope without undermining the contribution.
weaknesses: The central approximation remains empirically rather than theoretically justified. The unconditional ReTrack connection is well motivated, but the actual GUDA objective omits the density-ratio term, truncates to k-NN, uses finite fine-tuning, and adds preservation distillation; no formal bound relates the resulting unlearned model to the LOGO model.

The conditional text-to-image method is more heuristic. The weighted style-selection anchor construction is plausible and ablated, but it is not derived as a consistent approximation to the conditional LOGO objective, so the strongest counterfactual claims are less supported in the Stable Diffusion setting.

The Stable Diffusion LOGO oracle is itself a practical proxy: all models are fine-tuned from SD 1.5 rather than trained from scratch, and only 16 of 60 styles are used for evaluation. This is reasonable computationally, but it narrows the interpretation of the oracle and the generality of the conclusions.

The gains over strong baselines are meaningful but not overwhelming in all settings. On CIFAR-10, DAS is very close to GUDA on several metrics, and on UnlearnCanvas the absolute Top-1 agreement is 45.6% with low Spearman correlation, indicating that full ranking fidelity remains modest.

The CLIPA baseline is essentially free and surprisingly competitive on some ranking metrics. The paper argues convincingly that similarity is conceptually different, but the practical advantage of GUDA should be framed as head-attribution fidelity under a LOGO target rather than broad superiority for all use cases.

Reproducibility is mostly helped by detailed appendices, but the abstract leaves the code URL blank. Given the computational complexity and many implementation choices, public code/checkpoints or precise release details are important for others to reproduce the results.

The scope is limited to clean or mildly noisy disjoint groups, CIFAR-10 classes, and stylized image data. Overlapping styles, hierarchical groups, natural artist corpora, substantially larger model families, and more realistic copyright/consent settings remain untested.

The ethics discussion is minimal. Since the motivation includes copyright assessment and compensation, the paper should more explicitly discuss risks of over-interpreting attribution scores as legal or causal evidence, especially when the method only approximates a model-level counterfactual.
